subject: Climate & Environment
title: The West Antarctic Ice Sheet
description: A micro-lesson that makes The West Antarctic Ice Sheet usable.

hook.text: The West Antarctic Ice Sheet sits on bedrock below sea level. That makes it deeply unstable.

buildup.text: Warm ocean water is melting the ice from underneath, weakening its grip on the seabed.

discovery.text: Once ice retreats past a certain point on the underwater slope, collapse becomes unstoppable.

twist.text: Thwaites Glacier alone could raise seas by 65 cm — and it may have already passed its tipping point.

climax.text: Full collapse of West Antarctica would raise global sea levels by 3.3 meters over centuries.

punchline.text: The ice is melting from a place we can't see — and may not be able to stop.

quiz.question: Why is the West Antarctic Ice Sheet considered unstable?
options: It sits on bedrock below sea level
It is the warmest ice sheet
It is the thinnest ice sheet

details.summary: The West Antarctic Ice Sheet sits on bedrock below sea level, making it vulnerable to warm ocean water that melts it from underneath. It contains enough ice to raise global sea levels by about 3.3 meters and shows signs of instability that could trigger irreversible retreat.
details.whyItMatters: Collapse of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet would commit the world to meters of sea-level rise over centuries. Its marine-based geometry makes it uniquely vulnerable to runaway melting.
takeaways: The ice sheet sits on bedrock below sea level
It holds enough ice for roughly 3.3 meters of sea-level rise
Warm ocean water melts it from underneath, accelerating loss

faq.question: Why is the West Antarctic Ice Sheet especially vulnerable?
faq.answer: Its base lies below sea level on bedrock that slopes downward inland. As warm water melts the ice edge, the grounding line retreats into deeper terrain, exposing more ice to melting in a self-reinforcing feedback loop.

faq.question: Has retreat of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet already begun?
faq.answer: Yes. Glaciers like Thwaites and Pine Island are retreating faster than models predicted. Thwaites alone could contribute over 60 centimeters to sea-level rise, and scientists warn it may have already passed a tipping point.
